I spent the morning reviewing this patient's chart before the test and, honestly, the clinic was a mess: the scheduler double booked two sleep studies, the printer jammed twice, and the cafeteria ran out of coffee which did not help anyone's mood. The patient is a pleasant person who works as a carpenter, has two dogs, and recently moved to a new apartment near the lake, which apparently has a lot of dust from construction next door. We talked at length about their garden, the tomato blight this season, and whether the local baseball team will make the playoffs. Their sister visited last month from out of state and brought a casserole recipe that the patient described in great detail. Anyway, the interpretation: mild obstruction with FEV1 mildly reduced and normal FVC, TLC normal so no restriction, bronchodilator response not significant, DLCO normal when adjusted for hemoglobin. Other than that, I plan to follow up on the journal club article about hospital staffing ratios, which I have not yet read, and to remember to submit my conference abstract before the deadline on Friday, which I keep forgetting about every single week despite reminders from my chief resident and from the calendar app on my phone.

Yesterday was my first day back after the conference and I am still catching up on a mountain of emails, most of which are about parking permits, a vendor demonstration of a new electronic health record add-on, and the annual fire safety training that everyone ignores until the last day. The weather turned cold, my car needed an oil change, and I realized I had not eaten lunch until nearly four in the afternoon. A neighbor told me about a restaurant that serves excellent dumplings and I plan to try it this weekend with my family, assuming the babysitter is free and the traffic on the highway is not terrible because of the construction. In the meantime the actual test: moderate obstruction by FEV1 with a low FVC, lung volumes were not done so restriction cannot be evaluated, and there was a significant bronchodilator response; DLCO was not done. I also still need to find my reading glasses, return a library book that is now two weeks overdue, and reply to the committee about the schedule for next quarter's grand rounds before the weekend arrives.

We had a very strange afternoon in the lab: the humidity sensor was out of calibration, the new technologist was shadowing for the first time, and somebody left a half eaten sandwich near the spirometer, which prompted a long and slightly heated discussion about food policies in clinical areas. The patient is retired, plays cards on Thursdays, takes a walk around the block each morning with a neighbor, and mentioned a trip to the coast planned for early spring. We chatted about favorite novels, a local bakery that has changed its sourdough recipe, and the difficulties of finding parking near the medical campus on days when the farmers market is operating. Anyway, the actual result: normal FEV1/FVC ratio with a low FVC, TLC measured and low consistent with restriction, DLCO reduced, and no bronchodilator study was carried out. I should also mention that my own pager battery died, the elevator was out of service again, and I never did get to the stack of insurance letters that has been sitting on my desk since last Tuesday morning when everything started falling behind.

This patient was referred by a colleague in cardiology after a routine visit, and the paperwork came in late because the fax machine on the fourth floor has been unreliable for weeks. The patient is a schoolteacher who coaches a youth soccer team, drinks very little coffee, and was apparently quite nervous about the test because a friend had described it as exhausting. We talked about the best way to get to the hospital by bus, the new bike lanes, and why the downtown farmers market moved to Saturdays. Their dog recently had surgery and they were worried about leaving it alone for the day. Regarding the test itself: spirometry normal, TLC normal, DLCO normal, and no bronchodilator was given. The technologist graded the efforts as poor, so quality is limited and I would be cautious about subtle abnormalities. Separately, I have to renew my medical license by the end of the month, update my continuing education log, find a replacement for next Tuesday's clinic, and finally buy a birthday present for my niece, who will be eight and is currently obsessed with dinosaurs and space.

Today I helped a visiting medical student understand how the pneumotachograph works, which led to an extended digression about the history of respiratory physiology, the old water-sealed spirometers, and a story about a professor who used to carry a mercury manometer in his coat pocket. The lab also received a shipment of new mouthpieces, nose clips and filters, and half of the boxes were labeled incorrectly so we spent an hour sorting them. The patient arrived early, brought a thermos of tea, and told me about a vacation to the mountains that was cut short by bad weather and a flat tire on a very remote road. We also talked about gardening, about the cost of groceries, and about a television series that everyone at the clinic seems to be watching. For the record, the result was a low FVC and low FEV1 with a normal FEV1/FVC, a nonspecific pattern, and restriction cannot be confirmed because lung volumes were not measured; no bronchodilator was given and no DLCO was done. After that I went to lunch, attended a faculty meeting about parking, and drafted a long email regarding the upcoming holiday schedule for the whole division.

The respiratory therapist mentioned that the building air conditioning has been unreliable all week and the room temperature drifted well above what we prefer for testing, though she assured me the barometric pressure and temperature entries were updated properly. Our patient is a middle-aged bus driver who coaches a chess club on weekends, loves hiking, and gave up smoking nearly twenty years ago after a bet with his brother. We discussed the local election, the price of gasoline, and a documentary about deep sea creatures that he strongly recommended to me. His daughter is applying to colleges and the family is worried about tuition, which led to a surprisingly detailed description of financial aid forms. On to the findings: the FEV1/FVC ratio is reduced but FEV1 itself is within normal limits, so obstruction is present but I will not grade severity; TLC is normal, bronchodilator response was not significant, and DLCO is normal. I still need to order lunch, call the billing office about a denied claim, and finish the slides for Thursday's teaching conference about sleep apnea before the end of the day.
